'''Kenneth Mason Easley Jr.''' (January 15, 1959 – November 14, 2025) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who spent his entire seven-year career as a [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] for the [[Seattle Seahawks]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1981 to 1987. He played [[college football]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]] and was a three-time consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]]. He was selected by the Seahawks in the first round of the [[1981 NFL draft]]. Nicknamed "'''the Enforcer'''",<ref>{{cite web |title=Former UCLA, Seattle Seahawks safety Kenny Easley enters Hall of Fame at last |url=https://www.ocregister.com/2017/08/03/former-ucla-seattle-seahawks-safety-kenny-easley-enters-hall-of-fame-at-last/ |website=Orange County Register |date=August 3, 2017}}</ref> Easley has been considered among the greatest defensive backs of his era and as one of the Seahawks' greatest players.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1986 McDonald's Seahawks #45 Kenny Easley |work=McDonald's|publisher=McDonald's Corporation|year=1986|url=http://www.tradingcarddb.com/ViewCard.cfm/sid/9205/cid/914405/1986-McDonald's-Seahawks-45-Kenny-Easley|format=JPG|access-date=November 12, 2017}}</ref>

Easley was a leader of the Seahawks' defense<ref>{{Cite web|title=1987 Topps #183 Kenny Easley |work=Topps|publisher=Topps Chewing Gum, Inc.|year=1987|url=http://www.tradingcarddb.com/ViewCard.cfm/sid/3240/cid/817913/1987-Topps-183-Kenny-Easley|format=JPG|access-date=November 12, 2017}}</ref> and was named the [[NFL Defensive Player of the Year Award|NFL Defensive Player of the Year]] in 1984. He was a four-time [[All-Pro]] selection and was elected to the [[Pro Bowl]] five times in his career. Easley's career ended after the 1987 season when he was diagnosed with severe [[kidney disease]].

After retirement, Easley owned a [[Cadillac]] dealership and, later, the [[Norfolk Nighthawks]] team from 1999 to 2003. He was inducted into the [[Virginia Sports Hall of Fame]] in 1998 and was voted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2017.

He played for the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] from 2006 to 2007 and [[Green Bay Packers]] in 2008 and then shifted to the CFL, where he played for the [[Edmonton Eskimos]] in 2010 and the [[Calgary Stampeders]] in 2012.

'''Kenneth Wayne Sims''' (October 31, 1959 – March 21, 2025) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive end]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for eight seasons with the [[New England Patriots]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]], winning the [[Lombardi Award]] and [[UPI Lineman of the Year (College)|UPI Lineman of the Year]] en route to a victory in the [[1982 Cotton Bowl Classic]]. He was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2021.

'''Kenneth Bernard Bynum''' (born May 29, 1974) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for the [[San Diego Chargers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1997 to 2000. He played [[college football]] for the [[South Carolina State Bulldogs football|South Carolina State Bulldogs]] and was selected by the Chargers in the fifth round of the [[1997 NFL draft]] with the 138th overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1997 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1997/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In 1997, he played in 13 games, [[Rush (American football)|rushed]] 30 times for 97 yards and scored no [[touchdown]]s. In 1998, he played in 10 games and had 11 rushing attempts for 23 yards and 4 [[Reception (American football)|receptions]] for 27 yards. In 1998, he played in 16 games and had 92 rushing attempts for 287 yards and a touchdown to go along with 16 receptions for 209 yards and two touchdowns. In 2000, he played in 11 games and had only 7 rushing attempts for 26 yards and two receptions for 13 yards.

'''Kenneth Wayne Hill''' (born July 25, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player whose career lasted ten seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), from 1980 until 1989. Hill played for the [[Oakland Raiders|Oakland/Los Angeles Raiders]], [[New York Giants]], and [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and earned three [[Super Bowl]] rings, the first two with the 1980 and 1983 Raiders, the third with the 1986 New York Giants. Hill is the first and only [[Ivy League]] football athlete to have played on three Super Bowl championship teams.

Hill played college football at [[Yale University]], coached by [[College Football Hall of Fame]] member [[Carmen Cozza]]. Hill lettered three years, amassing 1594 rushing yards on 356 carries.<ref>http://www.sports {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130817042736/http://sports/ |date=2013-08-17 }} preference.com/cfb/players/Ken-hill-1.html</ref> He gained 910 yards rushing his junior year<ref>Yale University Official Football Program, October 27, 1979, [[Penn Quakers football|Pennsylvania]] Vs. Yale, "A New Pro Prospect Named Hill", pg. 15, by line Jon Stein, The [[New Haven Register]]</ref> and returned kickoffs and punts on special teams during three varsity seasons. Hill was named to the 1979 All-Ivy League First-team and 1978 All-Ivy League Second-team.<ref>[[The Harvard Crimson|Harvard Crimson]], "It's All-Ivy Time", November 28, 1978, by line John Donley</ref> Hill majored in Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry.<ref name="Bernstein2001">{{cite book|last=Bernstein|first=Mark F|title=Football: The Ivy League Origins of an American Obsession|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n3i4KOu7MiEC&pg=PA243|access-date=27 February 2016|year=2001|publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press|isbn=9780812236279|page=243}}</ref>

Hill had signed a letter of intent to play football at [[LSU Tigers football|Louisiana State]] for [[Charlie McClendon]], another member of the College Football Hall of Fame. Hill was recruited by LSU to play defensive back. "I can't blame him for going to Yale. He's very bright," McClendon remarked. Hill turned down football scholarship offers from, among others, the football programs at [[Baylor Bears football|Baylor]], [[Ole Miss Rebels football|Mississippi]], [[Mississippi State Bulldogs football|Mississippi State]], and [[Tulane Green Wave football|Tulane]].<ref>1979 Pennsylvania Vs. Yale program, pg.15</ref>

Hill, a varsity track letterwinner at Yale for Coach [[Lee Calhoun]], had been timed at 4.46 in the forty yard dash, and 9.7 in the 100 yard dash in college. Calhoun thought Hill could run a 9.5 in the 100 if he concentrated on track.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/22/obituaries/lee-calhoun-56-a-star-hurdler.html|title = Lee Calhoun, 56, a Star Hurdler|newspaper = The New York Times|date = 22 June 1989}}</ref>

Hill, like former Yale football athletes [[Don Martin (American football)|Don Martin]], [[Dick Jauron]] and fellow [[Super Bowl]] champion [[Gary Fencik]], converted successfully to [[defensive back]] in the NFL from running back or wide receiver.<ref>1979 Pennsylvania Vs. Yale program, pg.15</ref>
